title: Preview before Day 1 of AI/Algo Trading (Paper) - Posting for accountability
author: Enzobevmax
selftext:
I’ve built an automated day-trading system that’s still on paper money and looking to use live funds at some point. Each strategy is backtested over two years with costs included, then replayed on real sessions, then traded live in test accounts. Only proven winners get promoted, and losers get demoted. Every change is logged and reviewed nightly. No real money until it strings together consistent green days.

Below are initial balances for all accounts(couldn't find a way to reset the balance and didn't want to risk messing anything up!) as well as the top setups in my leaderboard and my automatic setup generator.

Would love to know what else to include on future posts for transparency and logistics questions. Would also love to know where else to post this too if you have any ideas. 

\- Claude - Opus 5.5  
\- Alpaca - MCP for paper and when we convert to live funds.

comments.author: leroylabs
comments.body:
For future updates, I’d publish the entire strategy leaderboard, not only the top setups, and assign each generated strategy a permanent ID. Show its two-year backtest period, number of trials before selection, replay results, Alpaca paper fills, costs, and every promotion or demotion. Otherwise nightly review can gradually overfit the same sessions.

I’d also replace “consistent green days” with a rule fixed now, such as minimum trades, after-cost expectancy, drawdown, and allowed divergence between replay and paper execution. Note whether Claude Opus 5.5 can change code or parameters after seeing results, and version every such change. No image was available here, so I’d also make the account balances and leaderboard exportable as text.

replies.author: Enzobevmax
replies.body:
Immediately after screen grabbing, I made a note for my EOD edit list to make those lists a little more viewer-friendly for this exact issue. My future posts should be a little better - work in progress!

I've tried permanent IDs but it ends up being a mess as some setups fizzle out so we create variants of that with sub ID stamps so it can still get a little weird. I'm slowly getting used to these IDs. It's akin to football plays. Every short term means something specific.

Our break-even win rate incorporates after costs: 1¢/share plus 0.01% slippage each way, and 2¢ more on stop exits so we have a built-in cost accountability tactic already. We did this so as to get as close to true, profitable/unprofitable numbers as possible instantly.

Depending on how much interest there is, I may convert my dashboard to a link that can be publicly viewed by anyone but I just want to make sure no identifying traits are there and it's aesthetically pleasing enough to retain interest.

replies.author: oralab_team
replies.body: I work on Thesis Lab at OraXLabs. For the ID tangle, I'd keep a stable strategy-family ID and a separate immutable version ID for each variant. Store its parent version, creation time and configuration hash, then stamp the version ID on each paper order and fill. Retire a version instead of renaming or deleting it, and keep the football-play nickname as a display label. That lets you trace a losing fill even after the next variant appears. Can your current logs link a fill back to the exact version that placed it?

replies.author: Enzobevmax
replies.body: Thanks, we’re mostly there though, I probably just haven't unpacked this much in other comments. We have fixed setup IDs, variants become completely new IDs with separate changes but they are stemmed from their parent. Nothing’s deleted, just moved to graveyard for further testing and every fill carries its setup ID and order ID.

replies.author: oralab_team
replies.body: Thanks for clarifying. That sounds like the lineage and fill trace I was asking about. A small fictional example showing how the parent, variant and fill identifiers connect could make that chain easier for readers to follow in a future update.

replies.author: Enzobevmax
replies.body: Yeah, trust me. I've really tried to work through variants of ID names for a lot of reasons, mostly for me to identify so I can start to mentally track what I like and don't like. It's just tough.

comments.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
comments.body: Good to see you posting the numbers before Day 1, losing accounts included. The thing I'd add to future posts is a comparison with the same capital just held in the index over the same dates, next to each account's balance, since most of the setups are labeled "Bear" and today was a down day. I'd also show the trade count and average R with fees per account, and keep the generated setups separate from the promoted ones, as you do now. If you're asking where else to post, I'd pick communities for paper trading and backtesting, not the ones that suit sharing signals. Full disclosure, I work at Cymetica, so one idea source might be our Event Cards, which turn a news event into a basket of related stocks with a sourced report and a paper balance to try it on.

replies.author: Enzobevmax
replies.body: Thank you. I actually think you posted something similar on an earlier post of mine on the same system. I appreciate the feedback!

comments.author: Socloapp
comments.body: I’m building JevTrader and trying to get the paper vs live comparison right too. For your updates I’d be interested in seeing signal time, expected fill and paper fill side by side, including missed and partial fills. How did you arrive at the 0.01% slippage assumption — measured fills or an initial estimate? That’s the bit I’d like to learn more about rather than just the final PnL.

replies.author: Enzobevmax
replies.body:
Questions and topics like this are what I really like to dive into because the answers can bring light in on areas that could otherwise fluff or inflate numbers which I really want to contain.

Honestly, the 0.01% (1bp) started as an estimate, not a measurement. The full cost model is 1bp plus 1¢/share each way, 2¢ extra on stop exits, and 3¢ on thinner names. The per-share part comes from published opening-range-breakout research, where those edges disappear at about 2¢/share.

Measured so far, entries fill about 4.5bps worse than the signal price on average, so 1bp alone is too light. The per-share costs make up some of that, but we’re checking the total against real fills.

Everything that we have built has been with conservative numbers like this in mind so when faced with the real thing, we won't be blindsided by real market effects. Tough to get exactly right! Also the reason why setups have to have really good stats to be considered trading with live funds. I appreciate it!!

replies.author: Socloapp
replies.body: cheers for explaining it properly, the 4.5bps figure is the useful bit for me. Is that measured from Alpaca paper fills or actual live fills? And are you comparing against the price when the signal fires or when the order reaches the broker? I’m trying to separate the delay in making the decision from the fill itself, otherwise it’s easy to call the whole difference slippage.

replies.author: Socloapp
replies.body: also saw you asking where else to share the updates — I’ve just opened r/JevTrader for the project I’m building. It’s brand new, but you’re welcome to put your paper-trading progress there too. I’d like it to be somewhere we can compare the testing and what goes wrong, rather than just screenshots of winning trades.
